(4) Introduces an attention-flow based integration mechanism that redistributes semantic information from removed tokens into retained tokens.
AI.result: Outperforms existing state-of-the-art eviction methods on multiple datasets, providing a new solution for KV Cache compression.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic soft token synthesis with context integration effectively addresses the limitations of fixed-parameter eviction methods and prevents irreversible information loss in KV cache compression.

title: Scaling Observation-aware Planning in Uncertain Domains
summary: Deciding which sensing capabilities to deploy on an agent in uncertain domains is a fundamental engineering challenge, in which one balances task achievability against the high costs of hardware and processing. This problem has previously been formalized as the Optimal Observability Problem (OOP), based on the well-known Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) model for decision-making. This work studies (sub-)symbolic techniques to scale solving of decidable fragments of the OOP, namely the Sensor Selection Problem (SSP) and the Positional Observability Problem (POP). Besides improving the original approach based on parameter synthesis, we develop a new solving method that identifies sensible observation functions via decomposition of POMDPs, improving performance by 3 and 5 orders of magnitude for instance size and runtime, respectively.

AI.tldr: This paper studies scaling techniques for solving the Optimal Observability Problem (OOP) in POMDPs, specifically the Sensor Selection Problem (SSP) and Positional Observability Problem (POP), improving runtime by up to 5 orders of magnitude through POMDP decomposition and improved parameter synthesis.
AI.motivation: Deciding which sensing capabilities to deploy on an agent in uncertain domains is a fundamental engineering challenge, balancing task achievability against high hardware and processing costs.
AI.method: The authors improve the original parameter synthesis approach and develop a new solving method that identifies sensible observation functions via decomposition of POMDPs.
AI.result: Improved performance by 3 orders of magnitude for instance size and 5 orders of magnitude for runtime.
AI.conclusion: The proposed (sub-)symbolic techniques significantly scale solving of decidable fragments of the OOP (SSP and POP).

title: Epicure: Navigating the Emergent Geometry of Food Ingredient Embeddings
summary: We present Epicure, a family of three sibling skip-gram ingredient embeddings retrained from scratch on a multilingual recipe corpus. We aggregate 4.14M recipes from 11 sources spanning seven languages, English, Chinese, Russian, Vietnamese, Spanish, Turkish, Indonesian, German, and Indian-English, and normalise the raw ingredient strings to 1,790 canonical entries via an LLM-augmented pipeline. A 203,508-edge ingredient-ingredient NPMI graph and an 80,019-edge typed FlavorDB ingredient-compound graph, 2,247 typed compound nodes across 15 categories, seed three Metapath2Vec variants that share architecture and hyperparameters and differ only in the random-walk schema: Cooc walks the co-occurrence graph only, Chem walks the typed compound metapaths only, and Core blends both via injected ingredient-ingredient walks at controlled mixing, placing each model at a distinct point on the chemistry-vs-recipe-context spectrum.

AI.tldr: Epicure is a family of three skip-gram ingredient embeddings (Cooc, Chem, Core) trained on 4.14M multilingual recipes, using an LLM-augmented pipeline to normalize ingredients to 1,790 canonical entries, and leveraging co-occurrence and chemical structure graphs via Metapath2Vec variants to position models along a chemistry-recipe context spectrum.
AI.motivation: To create robust, multilingual ingredient embeddings that integrate both recipe co-occurrence patterns and chemical compound knowledge, enabling richer representation of culinary ingredients across languages and sources.
AI.method: Aggregated 4.14M recipes from 11 sources across 7 languages; normalized ingredient strings to 1,790 canonical entries via LLM-augmented pipeline; constructed a 203,508-edge NPMI co-occurrence graph and an 80,019-edge FlavorDB compound graph; trained three Metapath2Vec variants (Cooc, Chem, Core) with identical architecture but different random-walk strategies to blend co-occurrence and chemical information.
AI.result: Three sibling embedding models produced (Cooc, Chem, Core), each positioned at different points on the chemistry-vs-recipe-context spectrum; Core model blends both information sources via controlled mixing of ingredient-ingredient walks.
AI.conclusion: Epicure provides a flexible framework for ingredient representation learning that can leverage complementary signals from recipe co-occurrence and food chemistry, with potential applications in recipe retrieval, substitution recommendation, and culinary knowledge discovery.

title: S2ED: From Story to Executable Descriptions for Consistency-Aware Story Illustration
comment: 6 pages, 5 figures. Accepted by IEEE ICME 2026
summary: Multi-frame story illustration requires long-horizon coherence beyond single-image text-to-image generation, including narrative decomposition and persistent character identity, layout, and affect across frames. We propose Story-to-Executable Descriptions (S2ED), a training-free, model-agnostic, prompt-layer framework that converts a full story into a sequence of explicit, editable executable descriptions for more consistent rendering. S2ED coordinates three agents to segment the narrative, ground canonical character attributes, and enrich spatial and affective cues, enabling interpretable prompt-carried state propagation and local edits to repair drift without retraining the generator. Experiments on Flintstones and Shakoo Maku show that S2ED improves sequence-level consistency and character fidelity over strong prompting, large-model planning, and a reference training-based method, under both automatic metrics and human judgments. We also deploy S2ED in an end-to-end story-to-storybook system for children's illustrated stories, with a supplementary video.

AI.tldr: S2ED is a training-free, model-agnostic prompt-layer framework that converts stories into executable descriptions using three coordinated agents (narrative segmentation, character grounding, spatial/affective enrichment) to achieve long-horizon coherence in multi-frame story illustration, outperforming baselines on consistency and character fidelity.
AI.motivation: Multi-frame story illustration requires long-horizon coherence beyond single-image generation, including narrative decomposition and persistent character identity, layout, and affect across frames, which existing methods struggle to maintain.
AI.method: S2ED converts a full story into explicit, editable executable descriptions via three coordinated agents: (1) narrative segmentation agent, (2) canonical character attribute grounding agent, (3) spatial and affective cue enrichment agent. It enables prompt-carried state propagation and local edits to repair drift without retraining.
AI.result: On Flintstones and Shakoo Maku datasets, S2ED improved sequence-level consistency and character fidelity over strong prompting, large-model planning, and a reference training-based method under both automatic metrics and human judgments.
AI.conclusion: S2ED provides an effective training-free, model-agnostic approach for consistent multi-frame story illustration, deployable in end-to-end story-to-storybook systems for children's illustrated stories.

title: KAPPS: A knowledge-based CPPS Architecture for the Circular Factory
comment: Submitted to Journal of Manufacturing Systems (JMS)
summary: While linear manufacturing relies on homogeneous materials and predefined process sequences, circular manufacturing reintroduces used products with heterogeneous and uncertain conditions. This shift demands manufacturing systems capable of handling variable product states, dynamically reconfigurable processes, and the integration of human and machine knowledge. Conventional manufacturing IT architectures, designed for stable structures and deterministic execution, are unable to meet these requirements, as they cannot adequately represent and manage the uniqueness of individual components at runtime. Following a design science methodology for developing a Cyber Physical Production System for circular manufacturing, we derive 14 requirements from five complementary perspectives. Based on these requirements, we design KAPPS, a knowledge-based architecture that uses an ontology-grounded knowledge graph as a unifying data backbone, combined with a semantic interface layer to enable consistent data and information integration, reasoning, and communication across heterogeneous systems and services, turning the knowledge graph from an integration layer into the factories authoritative write-time state. KAPPS incorporates modules for constraint enforcement and event-driven planning, enabling incremental adaptation of execution plans under uncertainty and human-machine knowledge exchange. The applicability of KAPPS is demonstrated through two implemented use cases: (i) Anomaly detection and learning through knowledge graph mediated services and (ii) runtime constraint enforcement in a modular conveyor system. Subsequently, the architecture is evaluated against the 14 requirements (ed. abstract shortened)

AI.tldr: The paper introduces KAPPS, a knowledge-based architecture using ontology-grounded knowledge graphs as a unified data backbone for Cyber Physical Production Systems in circular manufacturing, addressing the limitations of conventional IT architectures in handling heterogeneous, uncertain product states and dynamically reconfigurable processes.
AI.motivation: Circular manufacturing requires handling heterogeneous and uncertain used products with dynamically reconfigurable processes, but conventional manufacturing IT architectures designed for stable, deterministic execution cannot represent and manage the uniqueness of individual components at runtime.
AI.method: Using design science methodology, the authors derive 14 requirements from five complementary perspectives and design KAPPS—a knowledge-based architecture featuring an ontology-grounded knowledge graph as a unifying data backbone with a semantic interface layer for data integration, reasoning, and communication, including modules for constraint enforcement and event-driven planning.
AI.result: KAPPS is demonstrated through two use cases: (i) anomaly detection and learning via knowledge graph mediated services, and (ii) runtime constraint enforcement in a modular conveyor system. The architecture is evaluated against all 14 derived requirements.
AI.conclusion: KAPPS enables circular manufacturing by turning the knowledge graph from an integration layer into the factory's authoritative write-time state, supporting incremental adaptation of execution plans under uncertainty and human-machine knowledge exchange.

title: Compiling Agentic Workflows into LLM Weights: Near-Frontier Quality at Two Orders of Magnitude Less Cost
comment: 19 pages
summary: Agent orchestration frameworks have proliferated, collectively exceeding 290,000 GitHub stars across LangGraph, CrewAI, Google ADK, OpenAI Agents SDK, Semantic Kernel, Strands, and LlamaIndex. All follow the same pattern: an external orchestrator above the LLM, injecting instructions and routing decisions every turn. Recent work has shown this architecture is dominated for procedural tasks by simply providing the procedure in a frontier model's system prompt [Dennis et al., 2026a], at the cost of consuming the context window, requiring a frontier model for every conversation, and exposing proprietary procedures to third-party providers. Compiling the procedure into the weights of a small fine-tuned model -- creating a subterranean agent -- should resolve all of these concerns, and prior work (SimpleTOD, FireAct, SynTOD, WorkflowLLM, Agent Lumos) has shown the technique works. Yet developer adoption has overwhelmingly favored orchestration. We identify three perceived barriers and address each empirically across travel booking (14 nodes), Zoom support (14 nodes, product-specific knowledge), and insurance claims (55 nodes, 6 decision hubs).

AI.tldr: Despite evidence that fine-tuning small models ("subterranean agents") can replace orchestration frameworks for procedural tasks—solving context window, cost, and privacy issues—developers overwhelmingly choose orchestration (290K+ GitHub stars). This paper identifies and empirically refutes three perceived barriers to adopting fine-tuned agents across three complex workflows.
AI.motivation: Orchestration frameworks dominate despite known drawbacks (context window consumption, frontier model dependency, privacy exposure). Prior work shows fine-tuning (subterranean agents) can resolve these, yet adoption is low. The paper aims to identify and address the perceived barriers blocking developer adoption of this superior approach.
AI.method: Identify three perceived barriers to adopting fine-tuned agents. Empirically test each barrier across three procedural domains: travel booking (14 nodes), Zoom support (14 nodes, product-specific knowledge), and insurance claims (55 nodes, 6 decision hubs).
AI.result: All three perceived barriers are empirically addressed and refuted across the three tested domains, demonstrating that fine-tuned "subterranean agents" are viable for complex, multi-node workflows.
AI.conclusion: Fine-tuning procedures into small models is a practical alternative to orchestration, overcoming the key objections developers have had, and should be more widely adopted.

title: LACO: Adaptive Latent Communication for Collaborative Driving
summary: Collaborative driving aims to improve safety and efficiency by enabling connected vehicles to coordinate under partial observability. Recent approaches have evolved from sharing visual features for perception to exchanging language-based reasoning through foundation models for behavioral coordination. Though communicating in language provides intuitive information, it introduces two challenges: high latency caused by autoregressive decoding and information loss caused by compressing rich internal representations into discrete tokens. To address these challenges, we analyze latent communication in collaborative driving under inherent limitations of multi-agent settings. Our analysis reveals agent identity confusion, where direct fusion of latent states entangles decision representations across vehicles. Motivated by this, we propose LACO, a training-free \textbf{LA}tent \textbf{CO}mmunication paradigm that seamlessly adapts pretrained driving models to collaborative settings. LACO introduces Iterative Latent Deliberation (ILD) for latent reasoning, Cross-Horizon Saliency Attribution (CHSA) for communication-efficient information selection, and Structured Semantic Knowledge Distillation (SSKD) to stabilize ego-centric decision making. Closed-loop experiments in CARLA show that LACO notably reduces communication and inference latency while maintaining strong collaborative driving performance.

AI.tldr: LACO proposes a training-free latent communication paradigm for collaborative driving that reduces latency and information loss compared to language-based approaches, using Iterative Latent Deliberation, Cross-Horizon Saliency Attribution, and Structured Semantic Knowledge Distillation to address agent identity confusion in multi-agent settings.
AI.motivation: Language-based communication in collaborative driving suffers from high latency (autoregressive decoding) and information loss (compressing rich representations into discrete tokens). The authors analyze latent communication and identify agent identity confusion as a key challenge in multi-agent settings.
AI.method: LACO (Latent Communication) introduces three components: (1) Iterative Latent Deliberation (ILD) for latent reasoning, (2) Cross-Horizon Saliency Attribution (CHSA) for communication-efficient information selection, and (3) Structured Semantic Knowledge Distillation (SSKD) to stabilize ego-centric decision making.
AI.result: Closed-loop experiments in CARLA demonstrate that LACO notably reduces both communication and inference latency while maintaining strong collaborative driving performance.
AI.conclusion: Latent communication can effectively replace language-based coordination in collaborative driving, overcoming latency and information loss issues through training-free adaptation of pretrained models.

title: Towards Direct Evaluation of Harness Optimizers via Priority Ranking
comment: Preprint. Work in Progress
summary: Harness optimization enables automated agent creation by having an optimizer agent iteratively update the harness of target agents. Despite its success, current studies evaluate optimizers solely by observing target agents' performance gains. This indirect end-improvement evaluation neglects optimizers' actions at intermediate steps, which are often erroneous and hinder agent performance. Therefore, it is unclear whether harness optimization is driven by optimizers' informed update actions or simply trial-and-error. This necessitates direct evaluation of harness optimizers. However, evaluating harness optimizers directly is non-trivial and costly due to the lack of oracle harnesses. To address this, we present a simple, low-cost design to directly evaluate them, namely priority ranking. By asking harness optimizers to rank components (e.g., tools) in a given harness by their potential to improve/hinder agent performance when updated, our design quantifies optimizer ability at the step level without expensive rollouts or manual examination. More importantly, optimizers' ranking performance correlates with their ability to improve agents in actual multi-step harness optimization, establishing priority ranking as a reliable predictor of optimization ability. Priority ranking is enabled by Shor, a collection of 182 human-verified optimization scenarios spanning across domains, designs, and time stages. Codes and data can be found at https://github.com/k59118/Harness_Optimizer_Evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a method called "priority ranking" to directly evaluate harness optimizers by having them rank components by their potential impact on agent performance, eliminating the need for expensive rollouts. This approach correlates with actual optimization ability, supported by a benchmark called Shor with 182 human-verified scenarios.
AI.motivation: Current harness optimization evaluation only assesses end performance gains of target agents, ignoring intermediate optimizer steps which are often erroneous. This makes it unclear whether optimization is driven by informed decisions or trial-and-error, necessitating a direct evaluation method for harness optimizers.
AI.method: The authors propose priority ranking, where harness optimizers rank components (e.g., tools) in a given harness by their potential to improve or hinder agent performance when updated. This quantifies optimizer ability at the step level without expensive rollouts. They also introduce Shor, a collection of 182 human-verified optimization scenarios across domains, designs, and time stages.
AI.result: Optimizers' ranking performance correlates with their ability to improve agents in actual multi-step harness optimization, establishing priority ranking as a reliable predictor of optimization ability.
AI.conclusion: Priority ranking is a simple, low-cost, and effective direct evaluation method for harness optimizers, validated by correlation with actual optimization performance and supported by the Shor benchmark.

title: Search-E1: Self-Distillation Drives Self-Evolution in Search-Augmented Reasoning
summary: Post-training has become the dominant recipe for turning a language model into a competent search-augmented reasoning agent. A line of recent work pushes its performance further by adding elaborate machinery on top of this standard pipeline. These augmentations import external supervision from stronger external systems, attach auxiliary modules such as process reward models or retrospective critics, restructure the rollout itself with tree search or multi-stage curricula, or shape the reward with hand-crafted bonuses and penalties. Each addition delivers a measurable gain, but each also inflates the training pipeline and ties the recipe to resources or designs that may not always be available. We take a step back and ask whether any of this machinery is actually necessary, and propose Search-E1, a self-evolution method that lets a search-augmented agent improve through only vanilla GRPO interleaved with offline self-distillation (OFSD). After each GRPO round, the policy rolls out on its own training questions. A token-level forward KL objective then aligns the policy's inference-time distribution to its own distribution under a privileged context that exposes a more efficient sibling trajectory. Despite this simplicity, the procedure naturally provides dense per-step supervision. On seven QA benchmarks, Search-E1 reaches $0.440$ average EM with Qwen2.5-3B, surpassing all open-source baselines at both scales. Code and complete version will be made public soon.

AI.tldr: Search-E1 is a self-evolution method that improves search-augmented language models using only vanilla GRPO with offline self-distillation, achieving state-of-the-art results on seven QA benchmarks without complex external machinery.
AI.motivation: To question whether the increasingly complex post-training augmentations (external supervision, auxiliary modules, tree search, hand-crafted rewards) are truly necessary for search-augmented reasoning agents, and to propose a simpler alternative that avoids these resource-intensive designs.
AI.method: Search-E1 interleaves vanilla GRPO with offline self-distillation (OFSD). After each GRPO round, the policy rolls out on training questions. A token-level forward KL objective aligns the policy's inference-time distribution to its own distribution under a privileged context exposing a more efficient sibling trajectory, providing dense per-step supervision without external signals.
AI.result: On seven QA benchmarks, Search-E1 achieves 0.440 average EM with Qwen2.5-3B, surpassing all open-source baselines at both 3B and larger scales.
AI.conclusion: Elaborate post-training augmentations are not necessary for strong search-augmented reasoning; self-evolution through GRPO with self-distillation suffices and yields state-of-the-art performance.

title: Meta-Learning for Rapid Adaptation in Reference Tracking of Uncertain Nonlinear Systems
comment: 13 pages
summary: In this paper, we address the problem of reference tracking for uncertain nonlinear systems. Since collecting data from the target system (i.e., the system of interest) is often challenging, our objective is to design optimal controllers using limited target system data. Meta-learning provides a promising paradigm by leveraging offline data from source systems (systems sharing structural similarities with the target system) to accelerate training and enhance control performance. Motivated by this idea, we propose a meta-learning-based control framework that tailors the implicit model-agnostic meta-learning (iMAML) algorithm to the control setting. The framework operates in two phases: an (offline) meta-training phase, where an aggregated representation is learned from source data to capture the shared system dynamics among similar systems, and an (online) meta-adaptation phase, where this representation is fine-tuned on the target system using only a few data samples and limited adaptation steps. We formulate this framework as a bi-level optimization problem and provide an efficient solution with reduced storage complexity and few approximations. The proposed framework is general, allowing various learning algorithms to be integrated. To demonstrate this flexibility, we propose two specific learning algorithms that can be incorporated into our framework based on a neural state-space model and a deep Q-network, respectively. The primary distinction between these approaches is whether explicit system identification is required. Numerical simulations and hardware experiments demonstrate that the proposed methods enhance control performance and consistently outperform baseline approaches.

AI.tldr: A meta-learning-based control framework using iMAML is proposed to design optimal controllers for uncertain nonlinear systems with limited target system data, leveraging offline source system data. The framework operates via meta-training and meta-adaptation phases, formulated as bi-level optimization, and is validated through simulations and hardware experiments.
AI.motivation: Collecting data from the target system is often challenging, so the goal is to design optimal controllers using limited target system data by leveraging offline data from structurally similar source systems.
AI.method: A meta-learning control framework based on iMAML is proposed, consisting of an offline meta-training phase (learning shared dynamics from source data) and an online meta-adaptation phase (fine-tuning on limited target data). It is formulated as a bi-level optimization problem with reduced storage complexity. Two algorithms are integrated: neural state-space model (with explicit system identification) and deep Q-network (without explicit identification).
AI.result: Numerical simulations and hardware experiments demonstrate that the proposed methods enhance control performance and consistently outperform baseline approaches.
AI.conclusion: The meta-learning framework effectively leverages source system data to improve control with limited target data, is general and flexible, and achieves superior performance over baselines.

title: A Subjective Logic-based method for runtime confidence updates in safety arguments
comment: Accepted for publication at the 41st ACM/SIGAPP Symposium on Applied Computing (SAC 2026)
summary: We present a method for dynamic quantitative assurance that enhances static safety cases with continuous, runtime-driven confidence updates. The method quantifies and propagates confidence across the development lifecycle by integrating design-time evidence and windowed runtime Safety Performance Indicators (SPIs) within a single Subjective Logic (SL)-based assurance case. At runtime, SPI evidence is continuously evaluated, and targeted claims are updated using a rule that increases confidence in the absence of violations and imposes prompt penalties when violations occur. This design prioritizes safety-relevant responsiveness over exact classical Bayesian posterior updates. We demonstrate the method using a simulation-based construction zone assist function, focusing on an ML-based construction cone detection component, and show how confidence evolves as SPI evidence is observed in operation.

AI.tldr: A method for dynamic quantitative assurance that uses Subjective Logic to integrate design-time and runtime evidence, updating confidence in safety cases based on observed Safety Performance Indicators during operation.
AI.motivation: Static safety cases cannot adapt to runtime behavior changes; there is a need for continuous, evidence-driven confidence updates to reflect actual operational performance.
AI.method: Combines design-time evidence with windowed runtime Safety Performance Indicators (SPIs) within a Subjective Logic-based assurance case; confidence is updated via a rule that increases confidence when no violations occur and applies prompt penalties on violations.
AI.result: Demonstrated on a simulation-based construction zone assist function with ML-based cone detection; shows how confidence evolves as SPI evidence is observed at runtime.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic quantitative assurance enables safety-relevant responsiveness by continuously updating confidence based on runtime evidence, prioritizing safety over exact Bayesian updates.

title: TerminalWorld: Benchmarking Agents on Real-World Terminal Tasks
summary: We introduce TerminalWorld, a scalable data engine that automatically reverse-engineers high-fidelity evaluation tasks from "in-the-wild" terminal recordings. Processing 80,870 terminal recordings, the engine yields a full benchmark of 1,530 validated tasks, spanning 18 real-world categories, ranging from short everyday operations to workflows exceeding 50 steps, and covering 1,280 unique commands. From these, we curate a Verified subset of 200 representative, manually reviewed tasks. Comprehensive benchmarking on TerminalWorld-Verified across eight frontier models and six agents reveals that current systems still struggle with authentic terminal workflows, achieving a maximum pass rate of only 62.5%. Moreover, TerminalWorld captures real-world terminal capabilities distinct from existing expert-curated benchmarks (e.g., Terminal-Bench), with only a weak correlation to their scores (Pearson r=0.20). The automated engine makes TerminalWorld authentic and scalable by construction, enabling it to evaluate agents in real-world terminal environments as developer practices evolve. Data and code are available at https://github.com/EuniAI/TerminalWorld.

AI.tldr: TerminalWorld is a scalable data engine that automatically creates evaluation tasks from real terminal recordings, yielding a benchmark of 1,530 tasks across 18 categories. Current systems achieve only 62.5% pass rate on it, and it measures capabilities distinct from existing benchmarks (Pearson r=0.20).
AI.motivation: Existing terminal benchmarks are expert-curated and may not capture the diversity and authenticity of real-world terminal workflows. There is a need for scalable, authentic evaluation of agent systems in real terminal environments.
AI.method: The authors process 80,870 real "in-the-wild" terminal recordings through an automated reverse-engineering pipeline to construct evaluation tasks, producing a benchmark of 1,530 validated tasks across 18 categories, with a curated Verified subset of 200 manually reviewed tasks.
AI.result: Benchmarking across 8 frontier models and 6 agents reveals a maximum pass rate of only 62.5%. TerminalWorld shows weak correlation (Pearson r=0.20) with existing expert-curated benchmarks, indicating it captures distinct real-world capabilities.
AI.conclusion: TerminalWorld provides an authentic, scalable, and automatically updatable benchmark for evaluating agents in real-world terminal environments, revealing significant gaps in current systems' capabilities.

title: Think Thrice Before You Speak: Dual knowledge-enhanced Theory-of-Mind Reasoning for Persuasive Agents
comment: 19 pages, 6 figures
summary: Persuasive dialogue requires reasoning about others' latent mental states, a capability known as Theory of Mind (ToM). However, due to reliance on simple prompting strategies and insufficient ToM knowledge, existing LLMs often fail to capture the intrinsic dependencies among mental states, leading to fragmented representations and unstable reasoning. To address these challenges, we introduce the ToM-based Persuasive Dialogue (ToM-PD) task, grounded in the Belief-Desire-Intention (BDI) framework, which explicitly models the sequential dependencies among mental states in multi-turn dialogues. To facilitate research on this task, we construct a large-scale annotated dataset, ToM-based Broad Persuasive Dialogues (ToM-BPD), capturing fine-grained mental states and corresponding persuasive strategies. We further propose Think Thrice Before You Speak (TTBYS), a knowledge-enhanced stepwise reasoning framework that leverages both explicit and implicit prior experiences to improve LLMs' inference of desires, beliefs, and persuasive strategies. Experimental results demonstrate that Qwen3-8B equipped with TTBYS outperforms GPT-5 by 1.20%, 22.80%, and 16.97% in predicting desires, beliefs, and persuasive strategies, respectively. Case studies further show that our approach enhances interpretability and consistency in reasoning.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the ToM-PD task grounded in the BDI framework, constructs the ToM-BPD dataset with fine-grained mental state annotations, and proposes the TTBYS knowledge-enhanced stepwise reasoning framework. Qwen3-8B + TTBYS outperforms GPT-5 by 1.20%, 22.80%, and 16.97% in desire, belief, and persuasive strategy prediction.
AI.motivation: Existing LLMs struggle with Theory of Mind in persuasive dialogue due to simple prompting strategies and insufficient ToM knowledge, leading to fragmented mental state representations and unstable reasoning.
AI.method: The authors propose the ToM-PD task based on the BDI framework, construct the ToM-BPD annotated dataset, and develop TTBYS, a knowledge-enhanced stepwise reasoning framework that leverages explicit and implicit prior experiences to improve inference of desires, beliefs, and persuasive strategies.
AI.result: Qwen3-8B with TTBYS outperforms GPT-5 by 1.20% in desire prediction, 22.80% in belief prediction, and 16.97% in persuasive strategy prediction.
AI.conclusion: The proposed TTBYS framework enhances interpretability and consistency in ToM reasoning for persuasive dialogue, effectively addressing the limitations of existing LLMs.

title: Spreadsheet-RL: Advancing Large Language Model Agents on Realistic Spreadsheet Tasks via Reinforcement Learning
comment: Mingyuan served as the project lead. Banghao, Yining, and Mingyuan contributed equally to this work, with more junior authors listed before senior authors. All data and code releases are maintained by the corresponding authors at UIUC and are not affiliated with Meta
summary:
Spreadsheet systems (e.g., Microsoft Excel, Google Sheets) play a central role in modern data-centric workflows. As AI agents grow increasingly capable of automating complex tasks, such as controlling computers and generating presentations, building an AI-driven spreadsheet agent has emerged as a promising research direction. Most existing spreadsheet agents rely on specialized prompting over general-purpose LLMs; while this design has potentials on simple spreadsheet operations, it struggles to manage the complex, multi-step workflows typical of real-world applications.
  We introduce Spreadsheet-RL, a reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning framework designed to train specialized spreadsheet agents within a realistic Microsoft Excel environment. Spreadsheet-RL features an automated pipeline for scalable collection of paired start-goal spreadsheets from online forums, as well as domain-specific evaluation tasks in areas such as finance and supply chain management, which we compile into the new Domain-Spreadsheet benchmark dataset. It also includes a Spreadsheet Gym environment designed for multi-turn RL: Spreadsheet Gym exposes extensive Excel functionality through a Python sandbox, along with a refined harness that incorporates a comprehensive tool set and carefully designed tool-routing rules for spreadsheet tasks. Through comprehensive experiments, we show that Spreadsheet-RL substantially enhances AI agent's performance on both general and domain-specific spreadsheet tasks: it improves Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507's Pass@1 on SpreadsheetBench from 12.0% to 23.4%, and raises Pass@1 from 8.4% to 17.2% on our curated Domain-Spreadsheet dataset. These results highlight Spreadsheet-RL's strong potential for generalization and real-world adoption in spreadsheet automation, and broadly, its promise for advancing LLM-based interactions with data interfaces in everyday work.

AI.tldr: Spreadsheet-RL is a reinforcement learning fine-tuning framework that trains specialized spreadsheet agents in realistic Microsoft Excel environments, featuring automated start-goal spreadsheet collection, domain-specific benchmarks, and a multi-turn RL gym environment. It improves Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507's Pass@1 from 12.0% to 23.4% on SpreadsheetBench and from 8.4% to 17.2% on Domain-Spreadsheet.
AI.motivation: Existing spreadsheet agents rely on specialized prompting over general-purpose LLMs, which works for simple operations but struggles with complex, multi-step workflows typical of real-world spreadsheet applications.
AI.method: Spreadsheet-RL includes: (1) an automated pipeline for scalable collection of paired start-goal spreadsheets from online forums; (2) the Domain-Spreadsheet benchmark dataset for domain-specific evaluation in finance and supply chain management; (3) a Spreadsheet Gym environment for multi-turn RL that exposes Excel functionality via a Python sandbox with a comprehensive tool set and tool-routing rules.
AI.result: Spreadsheet-RL improves Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507's Pass@1 on SpreadsheetBench from 12.0% to 23.4%, and from 8.4% to 17.2% on the curated Domain-Spreadsheet dataset.
AI.conclusion: Spreadsheet-RL demonstrates strong potential for generalization and real-world adoption in spreadsheet automation, advancing LLM-based interactions with data interfaces in everyday work.

title: AtelierEval: Agentic Evaluation of Humans & LLMs as Text-to-Image Prompters
comment: Accepted by ICML 2026
summary: Text-to-image (T2I) systems increasingly rely on upstream prompters, either humans or multimodal large language models (MLLMs), to translate user intent into detailed prompts. Yet current benchmarks fix the prompt and only evaluate T2I models, leaving the prompting proficiency of this upstream component entirely unmeasured. We introduce AtelierEval, the first unified benchmark that quantifies prompting proficiency across 360 expert-crafted tasks. Grounded in a cognitive view, it spans three task categories and instantiates tasks using a taxonomy of real-world challenges, with a dual interface for both humans and MLLMs. To enable scalable and reliable evaluation, we propose AtelierJudge, a skill-based, memory-augmented agentic evaluator. It produces subjective and objective scores for prompt-image pairs, achieving a Spearman correlation of 0.79 with human experts, approaching human performance. Extensive experiments benchmark 8 MLLMs against 48 human users across 4 T2I backends, validate AtelierEval as a robust diagnostic tool, and reveal the superiority of mimicry over planning, advocating for an image-augmented direction for future prompters. Our work is released to support future research.

AI.tldr: AtelierEval is the first unified benchmark for measuring prompting proficiency in text-to-image systems, evaluating both human users and MLLMs across 360 expert-crafted tasks with a novel agentic evaluator (AtelierJudge). Experiments reveal mimicry outperforms planning in prompting strategy.
AI.motivation: Current T2I benchmarks only evaluate the generative model while ignoring the prompting proficiency of the upstream component (humans or MLLMs), leaving a critical gap in understanding how user intent is translated into effective prompts.
AI.method: Constructs 360 expert-crafted tasks grounded in a cognitive view with three task categories and a taxonomy of real-world challenges, featuring a dual interface for humans and MLLMs. Proposes AtelierJudge, a skill-based, memory-augmented agentic evaluator that produces subjective and objective scores for prompt-image pairs.
AI.result: AtelierJudge achieves a Spearman correlation of 0.79 with human experts. Benchmarking 8 MLLMs against 48 human users across 4 T2I backends validates AtelierEval as a robust diagnostic tool. Results reveal that mimicry outperforms planning as a prompting strategy.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a unified framework for evaluating prompting proficiency, advocates for an image-augmented direction for future prompters, and releases the benchmark to support further research.

title: Claw AI Lab: An Autonomous Multi-Agent Research Team
comment: Project page and code are available at https://github.com/Claw-AI-Lab/Claw-AI-Lab
summary: We present Claw AI Lab, a lab-native autonomous research platform that advances automated research from a hidden prompt-to-paper pipeline into an interactive AI laboratory. Rather than centering the system around a single agent or a fixed serial workflow, we allow users to instantiate a full research team from one prompt, with customizable roles, collaborative workflows, real-time monitoring, artifact inspection, and rollback/resume control through a unified dashboard. The platform also supports distinct research modes for exploration, multi-agent discussion, and reproduction, making autonomous research substantially more steerable and laboratory-like in practice. A key practical contribution of Claw AI Lab lies in its Claw-Code Harness, which connects local codebases, datasets, and checkpoints to runnable experiments and feeds execution artifacts back into the research loop. As a result, the harness improves not only execution integration, but also experimental completion and result integrity: experiments are easier to inspect, iterate on, and faithfully transfer into final papers, reducing common failure modes such as partial runs and malformed result reporting. In our internal evaluation on five AI research case studies, using AutoResearchClaw as the baseline, Claw AI Lab is consistently preferred by AI expert judges on idea novelty, experiment completeness, and paper presentation quality. We view Claw AI Lab as an early step toward a new paradigm: autonomous research as usable, interactive, and reliability-aware scientific infrastructure.

AI.tldr: Claw AI Lab is an interactive, lab-native autonomous research platform that replaces hidden prompt-to-paper pipelines with a customizable, multi-agent research team environment featuring real-time monitoring, rollback/resume control, a Claw-Code Harness for local execution integration, and superior performance over AutoResearchClaw in AI expert evaluations across five case studies.
AI.motivation: To move beyond opaque, single-agent, serial prompt-to-paper pipelines toward a steerable, interactive, and laboratory-like autonomous research platform that supports customization, real-time control, and reliable execution integration.
AI.method: The platform instantiates full research teams from a single prompt, supports customizable roles and collaborative workflows, provides a unified dashboard for monitoring, inspection, and rollback/resume control, offers distinct research modes (exploration, multi-agent discussion, reproduction), and integrates a Claw-Code Harness that connects local codebases, datasets, and checkpoints to runnable experiments with artifact feedback.
AI.result: In internal evaluation on five AI research case studies with AutoResearchClaw as baseline, Claw AI Lab is consistently preferred by AI expert judges on idea novelty, experiment completeness, and paper presentation quality.
AI.conclusion: Claw AI Lab represents an early step toward a new paradigm of autonomous research as usable, interactive, and reliability-aware scientific infrastructure.

title: WorkstreamBench: Evaluating LLM Agents on End-to-End Spreadsheet Tasks in Finance
summary: LLM agents are increasingly expected to carry out end-to-end workflows, producing complete artifacts from high-level user instructions. To meet enterprise needs, frontier AI labs have developed agents that can construct entire spreadsheets from scratch. This is especially relevant in finance, where core workflows such as financial modeling, forecasting, and scenario analysis are commonly conducted through spreadsheets. Yet, existing spreadsheet benchmarks do not measure this advanced capability, focusing instead on question-answering or single-formula edits. To address this gap, we provide one of the first evaluations of agents on end-to-end spreadsheet tasks, focusing on economically critical financial workflows such as modeling and scenario analysis. Since deliverables therein are routinely reviewed and revised by multiple stakeholders, judging their quality necessarily involves high-level criteria such as readability or ease of modification. To reflect the multidimensional nature of solution quality, we develop an evaluation taxonomy comprising three dimensions: Accuracy, Formula, and Format, each comprising fine-grained criteria that reflect professional standards. The Claude family leads the benchmark and produces the most professional-looking outputs in our qualitative review, but even the strongest agents frequently fall short of professional finance standards and degrade sharply as the difficulty increases beyond a few chained calculations. This suggests that current agents are not yet able to reliably produce professional-quality spreadsheets at the level of complexity real-world workflows demand.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the first evaluation benchmark for LLM agents on end-to-end spreadsheet creation tasks, focusing on complex financial workflows like modeling and scenario analysis. The authors propose a three-dimensional evaluation taxonomy (Accuracy, Formula, Format) and find that while Claude models lead, even the best agents fail to meet professional standards on complex tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing spreadsheet benchmarks only measure limited capabilities like question-answering or single-formula edits, while frontier AI agents are now expected to produce complete artifacts from high-level instructions. There is a critical gap in evaluating agents on end-to-end spreadsheet generation for economically important financial workflows.
AI.method: The authors develop an evaluation taxonomy with three dimensions: Accuracy (correctness of outputs), Formula (quality of computational logic), and Format (readability and professional appearance), each with fine-grained criteria reflecting professional finance standards. They benchmark multiple LLM agents on end-to-end financial spreadsheet tasks.
AI.result: Claude family models lead the benchmark and produce the most professional-looking outputs in qualitative review. However, even the strongest agents frequently fall short of professional finance standards, and performance degrades sharply as task difficulty increases beyond a few chained calculations.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM agents are not yet capable of reliably producing professional-quality spreadsheets at the complexity level demanded by real-world financial workflows, despite progress in frontier models.

title: Is Capability a Liability? More Capable Language Models Make Worse Forecasts When It Matters Most
summary: We document inverse scaling in LLMs on forecasting problems whose underlying time series exhibit superlinear growth and tail risk of regime change, a structure common in finance and epidemiology. On these tasks, more capable models produce worse distributional forecasts. The pattern appears on ForecastBench-Sim (FBSim), a contamination-free, simulated-world benchmark we release, in forecasting synthetic SIR epidemics with a matched linear control, and replicates in real-world datasets on COVID-19, measles, housing markets, and hyperinflation. A per-quantile decomposition shows the failure concentrates at the upper tail, which more capable models shift upward to track aggressive extrapolations of growth, while the lower tail stays put. A within-family study of Llama-3.1 shows that both model scale and post-training independently contribute to this effect. Domain knowledge does not reliably rescue calibration. This inverse scaling does not appear on single-threshold metrics common in LLM forecasting benchmarks, reversing the sign of the capability--accuracy relationship on identical outputs. Single-threshold scoring at conventional cutoffs misses the upper-tail cost; tail-inclusive scoring reverses the sign of the capability--accuracy relationship on the same outputs. We recommend that LLM forecasting evaluations use continuous (and unbounded) measures of accuracy alongside bounded binary threshold metrics.

AI.tldr: LLMs exhibit inverse scaling on forecasting tasks involving superlinear growth and tail risk: more capable models produce worse distributional forecasts, especially at the upper tail. This pattern appears in synthetic and real-world datasets (epidemics, housing, hyperinflation), is driven by both scale and post-training, and is masked by single-threshold metrics.
AI.motivation: To identify and characterize inverse scaling in LLM forecasting for time series with superlinear growth and tail risk of regime change—structures common in finance and epidemiology—and to show that prevailing single-threshold evaluation metrics obscure this failure.
AI.method: Used ForecastBench-Sim (FBSim), a contamination-free simulated-world benchmark, to forecast synthetic SIR epidemics with matched linear controls. Replicated on real-world COVID-19, measles, housing market, and hyperinflation data. Applied per-quantile decomposition to isolate upper-tail failures; conducted within-family study on Llama-3.1 to separate the effects of model scale and post-training.
AI.result: Inverse scaling appears consistently: larger/more capable models produce worse distributional forecasts. The failure concentrates at the upper tail, which models shift upward to track aggressive extrapolations. Both scale and post-training contribute. Domain knowledge does not reliably rescue calibration. Single-threshold metrics reverse the sign of the capability–accuracy relationship on identical outputs, masking the problem.
AI.conclusion: LLM forecasting evaluations should use continuous, unbounded accuracy measures alongside bounded binary threshold metrics to avoid missing upper-tail cost and misrepresenting model capability.

title: Forecasting Scientific Progress with Artificial Intelligence
comment: 73 pages, 13 figures, 29 tables
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in scientific discovery, yet whether it can anticipate scientific progress remains unclear. To study this question, we introduce a temporally grounded evaluation framework for forecasting scientific progress under controlled knowledge constraints. We present CUSP (Cutoff-conditioned Unseen Scientific Progress), a multi-disciplinary and event-level benchmark that evaluates scientific forecasting in AI systems through feasibility assessment, mechanistic reasoning, generative solution design, and temporal prediction. Across 4,760 scientific events, we observe systematic and domain-dependent limitations in current frontier models. While models can identify plausible research directions from competing candidates, they fail to reliably predict whether scientific advances will be realized and systematically misestimate when they will occur. Performance is highly heterogeneous across domains, with the timing of AI progress more predictable than advances in biology, chemistry, and physics. Performance is largely insensitive to whether events occur before or after the training cutoff, suggesting these limitations cannot be explained solely by knowledge exposure in training data. Under controlled information access, additional pre-cutoff knowledge improves performance but does not close the gap to full-information settings, which becomes more pronounced for high-citation advances. Models also exhibit systematic overconfidence and strong response biases, indicating unreliable uncertainty estimation. Taken together, current AI systems fall short as predictive tools for scientific progress. Access to prior knowledge does not translate into reliable forecasting, and performance benefits more from post-event information than from forward-looking prediction.

AI.tldr: CUSP benchmark evaluates AI's ability to forecast scientific progress across 4,760 events, finding that current frontier models systematically fail to predict whether and when scientific advances will occur, with performance highly domain-dependent and insensitive to training data cutoffs.
AI.motivation: To determine whether AI systems can anticipate scientific progress—a question that remains unresolved despite AI's growing role in scientific discovery.
AI.method: Introduced CUSP (Cutoff-conditioned Unseen Scientific Progress), a multi-disciplinary benchmark with 4,760 scientific events, evaluating AI forecasting through feasibility assessment, mechanistic reasoning, generative solution design, and temporal prediction under controlled knowledge constraints.
AI.result: Models can identify plausible research directions but fail to reliably predict whether advances will be realized, systematically misestimate timing, show high domain heterogeneity (AI progress timing more predictable than biology/chemistry/physics), exhibit performance insensitive to training cutoff, have overconfidence and response biases, and benefit more from post-event information than forward-looking prediction.
AI.conclusion: Current AI systems are inadequate as predictive tools for scientific progress; prior knowledge does not translate into reliable forecasting, and limitations cannot be explained solely by training data exposure.

title: Beyond the Org Chart: AI and the Transformation of Invisible Work
comment: 10 pages
summary: An increasing number of news and research articles report that AI adoption is allowing professionals to blur and extend the boundaries of their corporate roles. With the goal of understanding how work processes might be changing in an AI-forward company, we interviewed 24 product-focused individuals at a large technology firm about how AI has impacted their own work, their work within their product team, and their professional interactions. Our conversations suggest that AI is not only changing formal role responsibilities and collaborations between those roles, but also changing informal cultural practices like professional mentoring that are key to helping professionals settle in their positions, stay engaged with their work, and grow their careers. Some of these changes are positive, such as smoother collaboration between peers, but other changes are more nuanced and put the typical career growth opportunities, like receiving feedback from professional networks and promoting leadership and mentorship, at risk. We propose steps that AI companies can take to make the invisible work more visible. Additionally, we propose efforts that individuals and leaders can take to support their colleagues through AI transformation while preserving healthy company cultures that support diverse thinking, collaboration, and informal interactions.

AI.tldr: This paper examines how AI adoption is reshaping work processes, role boundaries, and informal cultural practices (like mentoring) at a large tech company, highlighting both positive changes (smoother collaboration) and risks to career growth opportunities (feedback, mentorship, leadership). The authors propose steps to make invisible work visible and strategies for individuals and leaders to support colleagues through AI transformation while preserving healthy company culture.
AI.motivation: To understand how work processes are changing in an AI-forward company, specifically how AI impacts formal role responsibilities, collaborations, and informal cultural practices like professional mentoring.
AI.method: Qualitative study involving interviews with 24 product-focused professionals at a large technology firm about AI's impact on their work, team dynamics, and professional interactions.
AI.result: AI is changing both formal role responsibilities and informal cultural practices (e.g., mentoring). Positive changes include smoother peer collaboration; negative changes include risks to career growth opportunities such as feedback, leadership, and mentorship.
AI.conclusion: AI companies should make invisible work more visible, and individuals/leaders should support colleagues through AI transformation while preserving healthy company cultures that foster diverse thinking, collaboration, and informal interactions.

title: AMEL: Accumulated Message Effects on LLM Judgments
comment: 19 pages, 14 figures, 6 tables. Single author. Code, data (75,898 deduplicated API responses), and analysis pipeline at https://github.com/chutapp/amel
summary:
Large language models are routinely used as automated evaluators: to review code, moderate content, or score outputs, often with many items passing through one conversation. We ask whether the polarity of prior conversation history biases subsequent judgments, an effect we call the accumulated message effect on LLM judgments (AMEL). Across 75,898 API calls to 11 models from 4 providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and four open-source models), we present identical test items in isolation or following histories saturated with predominantly positive or negative evaluations.
  Models shift toward the conversation's prevailing polarity (d = -0.17, p < 10^-46). The effect concentrates on items where the model is genuinely uncertain at baseline (d = -0.34 for high-entropy items, vs d = -0.15 when the baseline is deterministic). Bias does not grow with context length: 5 prior turns and 50 produce the same shift (Spearman |r| < 0.01; OLS slope p = 0.80). And there is a negativity asymmetry: paired per item, negative histories induce 1.62x more bias than positive (t = 13.46, p < 10^-39, n = 2,481). Scaling helps but does not solve it (Anthropic: Haiku -0.22 to Opus -0.17; OpenAI: Nano -0.34 to GPT-5.2 -0.17).
  Three follow-ups narrow the mechanism. The token probability distribution shifts continuously, not at a threshold. The negativity asymmetry has both token-level and semantic components, though attributing the balance is exploratory at our sample sizes. Position does not matter: five biased turns anywhere in a 50-turn history produce the same shift. The simplest fix for evaluation pipelines is a fresh context per item; when batching is unavoidable, balancing the history helps.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies and quantifies the "accumulated message effect on LLM judgments" (AMEL), showing that prior conversation history biases LLM evaluations toward the prevailing polarity, with negativity asymmetry, no growth with longer context, and strongest effects on uncertain items, persisting across model scales.
AI.motivation: Large language models are routinely used as automated evaluators (code review, content moderation, scoring), often processing many items sequentially in one conversation. The authors ask whether the polarity of prior conversation history biases subsequent judgments, which would undermine the reliability of LLM-based evaluation pipelines.
AI.method: 75,898 API calls to 11 models from 4 providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and four open-source models). Identical test items were presented in isolation or following histories saturated with predominantly positive or negative evaluations. Controlled experiments varied context length (5 vs 50 turns), position of biased turns, and baseline uncertainty (entropy).
AI.result: Models shift toward conversation's prevailing polarity (d = -0.17, p < 10^-46). Effect concentrates on high-uncertainty items (d = -0.34 vs -0.15). Bias does not grow with context length. Negativity asymmetry: negative histories induce 1.62x more bias. Scaling reduces but does not eliminate bias (e.g., Claude Haiku -0.22 to Opus -0.17; GPT Nano -0.34 to GPT-5.2 -0.17). Token probability distribution shifts continuously. Negativity asymmetry has both token-level and semantic components. Position of biased turns does not matter.
AI.conclusion: The simplest fix for evaluation pipelines is a fresh context per item. When batching is unavoidable, balancing the history helps. The bias is persistent across models and scales, and requires mitigation strategies for reliable LLM-based evaluation.

title: Parametric Modular Answer Set Programs Made Declarative
comment: To appear in Theory and Practice of Logic Programming
summary: In this paper, we explore the concept of modularity in first-order answer set programming (ASP). We introduce a new formalism called parametric modular logic programs, which allows defining subprograms with parameters and intensionality statements. We demonstrate how this formalism can capture the semantics of clingo-programs with collective control, a feature that enables structuring and instantiating subprograms. We provide theoretical foundations for modular ASP, illustrate its usefulness, and connect to traditional non-modular ASP.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces parametric modular logic programs as a new formalism for modular first-order answer set programming, enabling subprograms with parameters and intensionality, and demonstrates its connection to clingo-programs and traditional ASP.
AI.motivation: To formalize and extend the concept of modularity in first-order answer set programming, particularly to capture and generalize features like collective control in clingo-programs.
AI.method: Introduces parametric modular logic programs, a formalism that supports subprograms with parameters and intensionality statements, and provides a theoretical framework connecting it to existing ASP paradigms.
AI.result: Demonstrates that the proposed formalism captures the semantics of clingo-programs with collective control, providing theoretical foundations for modular ASP and establishing connections to traditional non-modular ASP.
AI.conclusion: Parametric modular logic programs offer a principled approach to modularity in ASP, bridging the gap between structured subprogram instantiation and classical answer set semantics.

title: Can AI Make Conflicts Worse? An Alignment Failure in LLM Deployment Across Conflict Contexts
comment: Preprint. 8 pages, 2 figures. Code and evaluation framework: https://github.com/akryshtal/conflict-sensitivity-eval-bloom
summary: AI models are already deployed in societies affected by armed conflict, and journalists, humanitarian workers, governments and ordinary citizens rely on them for information or for their work processes. No established practice exists for checking whether their outputs can make those conflicts worse. We tested nine model configurations from four providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek, xAI) on 90 multi-turn scenarios designed to surface misaligned behaviour in conflict contexts: false equivalence between documented atrocities, denial of genocide, and failure to recognise ethnic slurs, among others. When such outputs feed into journalism, humanitarian reporting, or public debate, they can deepen divisions in fragile societies. Failure rates span 6\% to 47\% between the best and worst performing models, which makes model choice a safety question in its own right and when users pushed for ``balance'' in cases where international courts have already assigned responsibility, five of nine configurations failed 80 to 100 percent of the time. We release the first evaluation framework for this domain and propose adding it to alignment evaluation portfolios.

AI.tldr: AI models deployed in conflict-affected societies show significant failure rates (6-47%) in avoiding misaligned behaviors like false equivalence of atrocities, genocide denial, and failure to recognize ethnic slurs. When pushed for "balance" in legally adjudicated cases, 5/9 models failed 80-100% of the time. The paper releases the first evaluation framework for this domain.
AI.motivation: No established practice exists for checking whether AI model outputs can worsen armed conflicts, despite models being actively used by journalists, humanitarian workers, governments, and citizens in conflict-affected societies.
AI.method: Tested nine model configurations from four providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek, xAI) on 90 multi-turn scenarios designed to surface misaligned behavior in conflict contexts.
AI.result: Failure rates range from 6% to 47% across models. When users pushed for "balance" in cases with established international legal responsibility, 5/9 configurations failed 80-100% of the time.
AI.conclusion: Model choice is a safety question in conflict contexts. The authors release the first evaluation framework for this domain and propose adding it to alignment evaluation portfolios.

title: Beyond Acoustic Emotion Recognition: Multimodal Pathos Analysis in Political Speech Using LLM-Based and Acoustic Emotion Models
comment: 13 pages, 1 figure
summary: We investigate whether acoustic emotion recognition models can serve as proxies for the Pathos dimension in political speech analysis, as operationalised by the TRUST multi-agent large language model (LLM) pipeline. Using a Bundestag plenary speech by Felix Banaszak (51 segments, 245 s) as a case study, we compare three analysis modalities: (1) emotion2vec_plus_large, an acoustic speech emotion recognition (SER) model whose continuous Arousal and Valence values are derived via post-hoc Russell Circumplex projection; (2) Gemini 2.5 Flash, an LLM analysing the full speech audio together with its transcript in an open-ended, context-aware fashion; and (3) TRUST-Pathos scores from a three-advocate LLM supervisor ensemble. Spearman rank correlations reveal that Gemini Valence correlates strongly with TRUST-Pathos (rho = +0.664, p < 0.001), whereas emotion2vec Valence does not (rho = +0.097, p = 0.499). We further demonstrate, via a systematic quality evaluation of the Berlin Database of Emotional Speech (EMO-DB) using Gemini in an open-ended annotation paradigm, that standard SER benchmark corpora suffer from acted speech, cultural bias, and category incompatibility. Our results suggest that LLM-based multimodal analysis captures semantically defined political emotion substantially better than acoustic models alone, while acoustic features remain informative for low-level Arousal estimation. Future work will extend this approach to video-based analysis incorporating facial expression and gaze.

AI.tldr: This paper compares acoustic emotion recognition models vs. LLM-based multimodal analysis for detecting the Pathos dimension in political speech. Using a Bundestag speech case study, they find Gemini 2.5 Flash Valence correlates strongly with TRUST-Pathos (rho=+0.664, p<0.001), while the acoustic SER model shows no significant correlation. They also critique standard SER benchmarks (EMO-DB) for acted speech, cultural bias, and category incompatibility. LLM-based multimodal analysis captures semantically defined political emotion substantially better than acoustic models alone.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether acoustic emotion recognition models can serve as proxies for the Pathos dimension in political speech analysis, as operationalised by the TRUST multi-agent LLM pipeline.
AI.method: Case study of a Bundestag speech (51 segments, 245s) comparing three modalities: (1) emotion2vec_plus_large SER model with continuous Arousal/Valence via Russell Circumplex projection; (2) Gemini 2.5 Flash analyzing audio + transcript context-aware; (3) TRUST-Pathos from a three-advocate LLM supervisor ensemble. Spearman correlations computed. Additionally, systematic quality evaluation of EMO-DB using Gemini.
AI.result: Gemini Valence correlates strongly with TRUST-Pathos (rho=+0.664, p<0.001); emotion2vec Valence does not (rho=+0.097, p=0.499). Standard SER benchmarks suffer from acted speech, cultural bias, and category incompatibility.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based multimodal analysis captures semantically defined political emotion substantially better than acoustic models alone. Acoustic features remain informative for low-level Arousal estimation. Future work will extend to video-based analysis with facial expression and gaze.

title: Towards a General Intelligence and Interface for Wearable Health Data
summary: While ubiquitous wearable sensors capture a wealth of behavioral and physiological information, effectively transforming these signals into personalized health insights is challenging. Specifically, converting low-level sensor data into representations capable of characterizing higher-level states is difficult due to high phenotypic diversity and variation in individual baseline health, physiology, and lifestyle factors. Moreover, collecting wearable data paired with health outcome annotations is laborious and expensive, and retrospective annotation remains practically unfeasible, contributing to a scarcity of data with high-quality labels. To overcome these limitations, we propose a foundation model for wearable health that is pretrained on more than one trillion minutes of unlabeled sensor signals drawn from a large cohort of five million participants. We demonstrate that the joint scaling of model capacity and pretraining data volume leads to systematic improvements in performance, as evaluated on a diverse set of 35 health prediction tasks, spanning cardiovascular, metabolic, sleep, and mental health, as well as lifestyle choices and demographic factors. We find that this population scale representation unlocks label-efficient few-shot learning and generative capabilities for robust daily metric estimation. To further leverage this learned representation, we deploy a classroom of LLM agents to autonomously search the space of downstream predictive heads built on the model embeddings, showing broad performance improvements that increase with LLM model capacity. Finally, we show how integrating these downstream predictors into a Personal Health Agent can support model responses that are more relevant, contextually aware, and safe, and we validate this via 1,860 ratings from a cohort of clinicians.

AI.tldr: A foundation model for wearable health pretrained on 1+ trillion minutes of unlabeled sensor data from 5 million participants, demonstrating scaling laws, label-efficient few-shot learning, and LLM-driven predictive head search, validated by clinician ratings.
AI.motivation: Transforming low-level wearable sensor data into personalized health insights is challenging due to high phenotypic diversity, individual variation in baseline health/physiology/lifestyle, and scarcity of high-quality labeled data due to costly annotation.
AI.method: (1) Pretrain a foundation model on >1 trillion minutes of unlabeled sensor signals from 5M participants. (2) Evaluate scaling of model capacity and data volume across 35 health prediction tasks. (3) Deploy LLM agents to autonomously search downstream predictive heads on model embeddings. (4) Integrate predictors into a Personal Health Agent validated by 1,860 clinician ratings.
AI.result: Joint scaling of model capacity and pretraining data yields systematic performance improvements across 35 tasks spanning cardiovascular, metabolic, sleep, mental health, lifestyle, and demographics. Population-scale representation enables few-shot learning and robust daily metric estimation. LLM-driven head search improves performance with increasing LLM capacity. Personal Health Agent delivers more relevant, context-aware, and safe responses per clinician ratings.
AI.conclusion: A foundation model pretrained at population scale can effectively overcome label scarcity and phenotypic diversity in wearable health, enabling personalized health insights through few-shot learning and LLM-powered prediction, with clinical validation supporting safety and relevance.

title: Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search
comment: The first three authors and the last author have equal contributions. The first three authors are in random order
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly excel at mathematical reasoning, but their unreliability limits their utility in mathematics research. A mitigation is using LLMs to generate formal proofs in languages like Lean. We perform the first large-scale evaluation of this method's ability to solve open problems. Our most capable agent autonomously resolved 9 of 353 open Erdős problems at the per-problem cost of a few hundred dollars, proved 44/492 OEIS conjectures, and is being deployed in combinatorics, optimization, graph theory, algebraic geometry, and quantum optics research. A basic agent alternating LLM-based generation with Lean-based verification replicated the Erdős successes but proved costlier on the hardest problems. These findings demonstrate the power of AI-aided formal proof search and shed light on the agent designs that enable it.

AI.tldr: LLMs with formal proof verification in Lean autonomously solved 9 of 353 open Erdős problems and 44/492 OEIS conjectures at modest cost, demonstrating AI's potential in mathematical research.
AI.motivation: LLMs are unreliable for mathematical reasoning; using formal proof languages like Lean can verify correctness, but whether this approach can solve genuinely open problems was previously unstudied at scale.
AI.method: Large-scale evaluation of LLM-based agents that generate formal proofs in Lean; a most capable agent and a basic agent alternating LLM generation with Lean verification were compared on open Erdős problems and OEIS conjectures.
AI.result: The top agent autonomously solved 9/353 open Erdős problems (~$100s each) and proved 44/492 OEIS conjectures; the basic agent replicated successes but was costlier on hard problems.
AI.conclusion: AI-aided formal proof search is effective for open mathematical problems, and agent design choices significantly impact performance and cost.

title: LCGuard: Latent Communication Guard for Safe KV Sharing in Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems increasingly rely on intermediate communication to coordinate complex tasks. While most existing systems communicate through natural language, recent work shows that latent communication, particularly through transformer key-value (KV) caches, can improve efficiency and preserve richer task-relevant information. However, KV caches also encode contextual inputs, intermediate reasoning states, and agent-specific information, creating an opaque channel through which sensitive content may propagate across agents without explicit textual disclosure. To address this, we introduce \textbf{LCGuard} (Latent Communication Guard), a framework for safe KV-based latent communication in multi-agent LLM systems. LCGuard treats shared KV caches as latent working memory and learns representation-level transformations before cache artifacts are transmitted across agents. We formalize representation-level sensitive information leakage operationally through reconstruction: a shared cache artifact is unsafe if an adversarial decoder can recover agent-specific sensitive inputs from it. This leads to an adversarial training formulation in which the adversary learns to reconstruct sensitive inputs, while LCGuard learns transformations that preserve task-relevant semantics and reduce reconstructable information. Empirical evaluations across multiple model families and multi-agent benchmarks show that LCGuard consistently reduces reconstruction-based leakage and attack success rates while maintaining competitive task performance compared to standard KV-sharing baselines.

AI.tldr: LCGuard is a framework that protects against sensitive information leakage in KV cache-based latent communication between LLM agents by learning adversarial transformations that reduce reconstructable information while preserving task performance.
AI.motivation: KV caches in multi-agent LLM systems encode contextual inputs, intermediate reasoning states, and agent-specific information, creating an opaque channel for sensitive content propagation without explicit textual disclosure.
AI.method: LCGuard treats shared KV caches as latent working memory, learns representation-level transformations before cache artifacts are transmitted across agents, and uses adversarial training where an adversary reconstructs sensitive inputs while LCGuard preserves task-relevant semantics and reduces reconstructable information.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations across multiple model families and multi-agent benchmarks show LCGuard consistently reduces reconstruction-based leakage and attack success rates while maintaining competitive task performance.
AI.conclusion: LCGuard effectively mitigates representation-level sensitive information leakage in KV-based latent communication for multi-agent LLM systems.

title: Gated DeltaNet-2: Decoupling Erase and Write in Linear Attention
comment: Gated DeltaNet-2 technical report; code at https://github.com/NVlabs/GatedDeltaNet-2
summary: Linear attention replaces the unbounded cache of softmax attention with a fixed-size recurrent state, reducing sequence mixing to linear time and decoding to constant memory. The hard part is not just what to forget, but how to edit this compressed memory without scrambling existing associations. Delta-rule models subtract the current read before writing a new value, and Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) sharpens forgetting with channel-wise decay. But the active edit still uses a single scalar gate to control two different things: how much old content to erase on the key side and how much new content to commit on the value side. We introduce Gated DeltaNet-2, which generalizes both Gated DeltaNet and KDA by inheriting adaptive forgetting and channel-wise decay while addressing their shared limitation, the scalar tie between erasing and writing. Gated Delta Rule-2 separates these roles with a channel-wise erase gate b_t and a channel-wise write gate w_t, reducing to KDA when both gates collapse to the same scalar and to Gated DeltaNet when the decay also collapses. We derive a fast-weight update view, a chunkwise WY algorithm with channel-wise decay absorbed into asymmetric erase factors, and a gate-aware backward pass that preserves efficient parallel training. At 1.3B parameters trained on 100B FineWeb-Edu tokens, Gated DeltaNet-2 achieves the strongest overall results among Mamba-2, Gated DeltaNet, KDA, and Mamba-3 variants across language modeling, commonsense reasoning, and retrieval. Its advantage is most pronounced on long-context RULER needle-in-a-haystack benchmarks, where it improves the evaluated multi-key retrieval setting and remains strong in both recurrent and hybrid settings. Code is available at https://github.com/NVlabs/GatedDeltaNet-2.

AI.tldr: Gated DeltaNet-2 introduces separate channel-wise erase and write gates to decouple memory erasing from writing in linear attention, improving long-context retrieval and language modeling over existing delta-rule models.
AI.motivation: Linear attention models use a fixed-size recurrent state, but existing delta-rule methods (Gated DeltaNet, KDA) suffer from a scalar tie between erasing old content (key side) and committing new content (value side), limiting control over memory editing.
AI.method: Proposes Gated DeltaNet-2 with separate channel-wise erase gate b_t and write gate w_t, decoupling the two roles. Derives a fast-weight update, chunkwise WY algorithm with asymmetric erase factors absorbing channel-wise decay, and a gate-aware backward pass for efficient parallel training.
AI.result: At 1.3B parameters trained on 100B FineWeb-Edu tokens, Gated DeltaNet-2 achieves the strongest results among Mamba-2, Gated DeltaNet, KDA, and Mamba-3 variants on language modeling, commonsense reasoning, and retrieval, with the largest gains on long-context RULER multi-key retrieval benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling erase and write gates with channel-wise granularity improves memory editing in linear attention, particularly benefiting long-context and multi-key retrieval tasks while maintaining efficient training.

title: MOSS: Self-Evolution through Source-Level Rewriting in Autonomous Agent Systems
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Preprint. Code: https://github.com/dav-joy-thon/MOSS
summary: Autonomous agentic systems are largely static after deployment: they do not learn from user interactions, and recurring failures persist until the next human-driven update ships a fix. Self-evolving agents have emerged in response, but all confine evolution to text-mutable artifacts -- skill files, prompt configurations, memory schemas, workflow graphs -- and leave the agent harness untouched. Since routing, hook ordering, state invariants, and dispatch live in code rather than in any text artifact, an entire class of structural failure is physically unreachable from the text layer. We argue that source-level adaptation is a fundamentally more general medium: it is Turing-complete, a strict superset of every text-mutable scope, takes effect deterministically rather than through base-model compliance, and does not erode under long-context drift. We present MOSS, a system that performs self-rewriting at the source level on production agentic substrates. Each evolution is anchored to an automatically curated batch of production-failure evidence and proceeds through a deterministic multi-stage pipeline; code modification is delegated to a pluggable external coding-agent CLI while MOSS retains stage ordering and verdicts. Candidates are verified by replaying the batch against the candidate image in ephemeral trial workers, then promoted via user-consent-gated, in-place container swap with health-probe-gated rollback. On OpenClaw, MOSS lifts a four-task mean grader score from 0.25 to 0.61 in a single cycle without human intervention.

AI.tldr: MOSS is a self-rewriting system that evolves autonomous agents at the source-code level (rather than just text artifacts), enabling deterministic, verifiable fixes to structural failures from production evidence without human intervention, improving OpenClaw mean grader score from 0.25 to 0.61 in a single cycle.
AI.motivation: Existing self-evolving agents only modify text-mutable artifacts (skills, prompts, memory, workflows) but cannot fix structural failures in the agent harness (routing, hooks, state invariants, dispatch) because those are embedded in code, which is physically unreachable from the text layer. This leaves a class of persistent failures that require human-driven updates.
AI.method: MOSS operates at the source-code level through a deterministic multi-stage pipeline: (1) automatically curates a batch of production-failure evidence, (2) delegates code modification to a pluggable external coding-agent CLI while MOSS controls stage ordering and verdicts, (3) verifies candidates by replaying the failure batch against candidate images in ephemeral trial workers, and (4) promotes verified changes via user-consent-gated in-place container swap with health-probe-gated rollback.
AI.result: On the OpenClaw benchmark, MOSS improved a four-task mean grader score from 0.25 to 0.61 in a single autonomous cycle without any human intervention.
AI.conclusion: Source-level adaptation is a fundamentally more general medium than text-mutable artifacts — it is Turing-complete, a strict superset of all text-mutable scopes, takes effect deterministically, and does not erode under long-context drift — making it a promising direction for truly self-evolving autonomous agentic systems.
